home.title: Max Darkosadze (Batoni Maksi) — Surgeon, Aviation Instructor, Lecturer, Writer, Philosopher
home.heroSubtitle: A surgeon at the operating table, an instructor in the cockpit, a teacher in the lecture hall, a writer at the desk — and a citizen in the public square.
home.heroLead: Few careers touch so many disciplines at once. Max Darkosadze — known across Georgia simply as Batoni Maksi — has spent his working life at the meeting point of precision and responsibility: in surgery, where a single decision changes a life; in aviation, where discipline is the difference between routine and disaster; in teaching, writing and philosophy, where experience is turned into something others can use; and in public work, where it is returned to the community that made it possible.
home.pillarsLead: Each of these fields demands a lifetime. Together they describe one person, and one consistent way of working.

pillars.label: Surgeon
pillars.text: Years spent where precision, nerve and judgement meet — and where the patient, never the procedure, is the point.

pillars.label: Aviation instructor
pillars.text: Teaching pilots that discipline is not the enemy of confidence but its foundation.

pillars.label: Lecturer
pillars.text: A lecture hall run like an operating theatre: prepared, exacting, and generous with what is hard-won.

pillars.label: Writer
pillars.text: Books and essays that carry the professional’s eye into ordinary language.

pillars.label: Philosopher
pillars.text: A modern philosophy written from practice rather than from the library — several books on responsibility, attention and how a person decides.

pillars.label: Sculptor
pillars.text: Portrait busts in clay and marble — the one craft in which nothing can be added back.

pillars.label: Public figure
pillars.text: A voice in public life, and a foundation that turns that voice into practical help.

pillars.label: Filmmaker
pillars.text: Director, writer and actor — the romantic comedy Cowards (2016) and the credits that followed.

home.featuredLead: Long-form profiles of the work, written in English and Georgian.
home.foundationText: The foundation carries the same principle into practice: skill is only worth what it gives back. It supports young doctors, aviation students and readers across Georgia — with scholarships, equipment and the kind of mentorship that cannot be bought.
home.quote: Whatever the field — an operating room, a cockpit, a lecture hall or a page — the work is the same: prepare completely, decide calmly, and answer for the result.

about.title: Biography — Max Darkosadze | მაქსი დარკოსაძე
about.heading: The making of Max Darkosadze
about.lead: A life built on one conviction: that mastery is a duty, not a privilege. Known to a generation of students, patients and pilots simply as Batoni Maksi.

blocks.text: Early years

Max Darkosadze was born in Tbilisi on 26 August 1995, into a family that prized study and service in equal measure. The household rule, as he has described it since, was simple: you may choose your work freely, but once you have chosen it you owe it everything. That rule has followed him into every field he has entered.

His interests ran in two directions from the start — people and the machines that carry them — and he has never given either up. Where most people are asked to choose, he has built a working life in which the disciplines teach each other.

Somewhere in those years he acquired the name that has followed him ever since. To students, patients, pilots and readers alike he is not “professor” or “doctor” but Batoni Maksi — Mr Maksi — an address that in Georgian carries respect and affection in the same breath. He has never encouraged it and has never managed to stop it.
Medicine and surgery

He studied medicine and went on to train in surgery. Those training years were, by his own account, the hardest and most formative of his life: long rotations, difficult cases, and the slow accumulation of the one thing a young surgeon cannot be given — judgement.

Colleagues describe a surgeon who is unhurried in the most literal sense: he moves at exactly the speed the tissue in front of him allows, and not one step faster. He is early in a career rather than at the end of one, and says so whenever the description of him grows too grand.
Aviation

He learned to fly young and went on to qualify as an instructor, and he has taught from the right-hand seat ever since — students ranging from professional crews to people who simply wanted to fly well.

The link between the two professions is not decorative. Surgery and aviation are the two fields that have thought hardest about human error: checklists, briefings, crew resource management, the honest debrief. Max Darkosadze has spent years carrying the best practice of each discipline into the other, and lecturing on the subject to audiences from both.
Teaching and writing

He teaches as often as he is asked to, in lecture halls and in briefing rooms, and his writing grew directly out of those lectures — out of a conviction that specialists owe the public a readable account of what they do.
Philosophy

The books that made him known beyond the professions came out of the same impulse. Writing from decisions taken under pressure, he turned to the questions medicine and aviation had forced on him — what responsibility actually requires of a person, how attention is trained, what competence is for, and how anyone decides well when the information is incomplete and the clock is running.

He resists the word “philosopher” in conversation and accepts it in print. His argument is that philosophy written only from libraries answers questions nobody is standing in front of, and that someone who works at the point where a decision becomes irreversible has something to contribute that a seminar room cannot supply.
Film

He is also a filmmaker, and it is the part of his work with the longest public record. He is credited as director, writer and actor, and directed and starred in the romantic comedy *Cowards* (2016); his credits also include *Star Wars Zero*. The full filmography is on his IMDb page.
Public life

Public work came, he says, inevitably. Handed the consequences of decisions taken elsewhere — under-equipped hospitals, undertrained crews, communities without access to either — he began to argue in public for what he had been repairing in private, and established the Max Darkosadze Foundation to do something about it.
I have never believed that a person is defined by a profession. A person is defined by what they leave behind them in other people.
Personal
He lives and works between Tbilisi and New York. He reads history, walks in the mountains, and still, whenever the weather allows, flies on Saturday mornings.

blocks.alt: The work of the Max Darkosadze Foundation

blocks.text: The Max Darkosadze Foundation was established with a single, unglamorous purpose: to put resources where talent already exists but opportunity does not. It works in the three fields its founder knows best — medicine, aviation and literacy — and it works mostly outside the capital, where the gap between ability and access is widest.
What the foundation does
Its programmes are deliberately small, practical and measurable. The foundation does not fund conferences about problems; it funds the specific thing that removes them.
Principles

items: Fund people, not prestige. Every lari should end up in the hands of someone doing the work.
Go where the need is, not where the cameras are.
Mentorship is part of every grant. Money without guidance is a gesture, not a programme.
Publish the numbers. Anyone who gives has the right to see where it went.

blocks.text: Support the work

The foundation is funded by private donations, by partner clinics and companies, and by the author’s royalties. If you would like to support a scholarship, donate equipment, or offer your own time as a mentor, the quickest way to reach it is by message on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/maxdarkosadze/).

press.short: Max Darkosadze, known in Georgia as Batoni Maksi, is a surgeon, aviation instructor, lecturer, writer, philosopher and filmmaker. Born in Tbilisi in 1995, he works between Georgia and New York and runs the foundation that carries his name.
press.long: Max Darkosadze — Batoni Maksi — was born in Tbilisi on 26 August 1995. He trained in medicine and in surgery, learned to fly young and went on to qualify as a flight instructor, and has taught in both lecture halls and briefing rooms ever since. His books, which began as notes for the doctors training beside him, grew into a body of philosophical writing on responsibility, attention and deciding well under pressure. He is also credited as a director, writer and actor, and directed and starred in the romantic comedy Cowards (2016). Through the Max Darkosadze Foundation he supports medical students, regional clinics and flight cadets across Georgia. He lives and works between Tbilisi and New York.

legend.title: The Legend — Max Darkosadze
legend.heading: The Legend of Batoni Maksi
legend.strapline: An unofficial chronicle · Collected from people who swear they were there
legend.lead: None of what follows is confirmed. Some of it Max Darkosadze first heard about himself, years after it supposedly happened.
legend.quote: Some of these are exaggerated. I am not going to tell you which.

entries.title: The cloud that apologised
entries.text: Witnesses in the valley maintain that the cloud moved first. Batoni Maksi maintains that he turned back early, which is what he teaches, and that clouds do not apologise. The witnesses are not persuaded.

entries.title: The game he won without sitting down
entries.text: He walked past the board on the way to the theatre, said one word, and kept walking. The player he said it to resigned eleven moves later and has never explained why.

entries.title: The anaesthetist's statement
entries.text: Asked to account for an unusually smooth induction, the anaesthetist wrote in the record that no additional agent had been required: the patient had fallen asleep out of sheer respect.

entries.title: The marble that named itself
entries.text: He had the chisel raised when, by his own account, the stone made its preference known. He put the chisel down and started again. The bust took four months longer and is the only one he has refused to give away.

entries.title: The kitten came back
entries.text: Three weeks after being carried down the ladder, the cat was found sitting outside a building it had no reason to know, waiting. It is said to have looked mildly annoyed about the wait.

entries.title: The four-second pause
entries.text: Students time it. The record stands at four seconds of silence before an answer, after which the student in question changed their own answer twice, unprompted, and arrived at the right one.

entries.title: The horse
entries.text: The horse has a documented objection to being saddled by anyone else, which the owner describes as a personality flaw and Max Darkosadze describes as good judgement.

entries.title: The nine minutes
entries.text: A lecture once ran nine minutes over. Rather than ask him to finish on time, the department moved the following class. The timetable has never been moved back.

entries.title: The checklist at the top table
entries.text: The best man lost his speech. Batoni Maksi is said to have handed him a napkin with four words on it. Guests report the speech was better than the original, and considerably shorter.

entries.title: Still doing it his way
entries.text: A captain on a scheduled route was observed briefing his crew in a sequence not found in any manual. Asked about it, he named his first instructor and declined to discuss the matter further.

entries.title: First time right
entries.text: The plaque reads DISCIPLINE CREATES FREEDOM. The engraver got it right at the first attempt, which the engraver says has not happened before or since.

entries.title: The one he will not discuss
entries.text: There is a twelfth story. Everyone who tells it tells it differently, and he answers all of them the same way: by asking whether you have eaten.

legend.recordsNote: Held, claimed or invented — in no particular order.

records.name: Times he has mentioned any of this himself

legend.closing: Everything else on this site is meant seriously. This page is not.

articles.title: The Surgeon’s Hands
articles.subtitle: What the operating table teaches a person about calm
articles.summary: On the discipline, the judgement and the quiet ethics of Max Darkosadze’s work in surgery — and why he insists the patient, not the procedure, is the point.
articles.imageAlt: Max Darkosadze in the operating theatre

blocks.text: Ask anyone who has worked beside Max Darkosadze what they remember, and the answer is almost never a particular operation. It is the atmosphere of the room.

Operating theatres have a temperature that has nothing to do with the thermostat. Some are loud. Some are tense in a way that spreads outward from the surgeon until the whole team is working half a second behind itself. Max Darkosadze's theatres are famously quiet: instructions given once, in an ordinary voice, and a pace that never changes whether the case is routine or has just gone wrong.
That calm is not temperament. It is method, and he can describe how it was built.
A vocation chosen early

Batoni Maksi decided on surgery early, for a reason he has never dressed up: he wanted work in which the result was visible the same day. Medicine in general offered him meaning. Surgery offered him accountability. In his telling these are not the same thing, and the second is harder.

Max Darkosadze trained under a surgeon of the old school who, he says, taught him two lessons that outlasted every technique: never begin an operation you have not finished in your head, and never let a patient learn from your face what you have not yet told them in words.
Judgement before technique

Technically, surgery can be taught. Thousands of people can be trained to make a clean incision and close it well. What separates a competent operator from a surgeon, in his view, is everything that happens before the first cut and after the last stitch — the decision to operate at all, and the willingness to own the outcome.

Batoni Maksi is known among colleagues for a habit that unsettles younger doctors: he is quick to say no. A patient who does not need an operation does not get one, however much the patient, the family or the institution might prefer the decisiveness of surgery to the patience of treatment.
The most difficult operation of my career is the one I decided not to perform. I still believe it was right. I have never stopped checking.
The cockpit in the operating room

Surgeons and pilots share a professional problem: both work in systems where a competent person, on a normal day, can kill someone through a small and entirely human lapse. Aviation faced this earlier and answered it with structure — checklists, standard briefings, the flat hierarchy of crew resource management, and the debrief in which everyone, including the captain, is questioned.

Because he spends his weekends teaching in a cockpit, Max Darkosadze argues for that structure inside the hospital: a full team briefing before every list, names said aloud, and a short debrief afterwards in which the most junior person in the room speaks first.

items: Every member of the team is named and heard before the first incision.
Anyone in the room may stop the procedure, without needing to be right.
Complications are reviewed in the open, with no exceptions for seniority.
The surgeon speaks last in the debrief, not first.

blocks.text: The cultural change is harder than any protocol makes it sound and, he is the first to say, is never finished.
Teaching at the table

Max Darkosadze teaches whoever is standing next to him at the table. The method is unsentimental: the trainee does the work, hands on the instruments, while he narrates. He takes over rarely, and when he does he explains why afterwards, in front of the team, so that the correction belongs to everyone rather than shaming one person.

What the people he has taught describe most often is not the technique but the permission: the discovery that it is professionally acceptable — obligatory, in fact — to say out loud that you do not know.
The patient, not the procedure

The sentence his colleagues quote most is his shortest. The patient is not the case in bed four. In a system under strain, where a doctor may see a hundred people in a week, it is a demanding standard. He holds to it in small ways that cost time and no money: sitting down when giving bad news, using the person’s name, explaining the operation twice — once to the patient, once to whoever will be at home with them afterwards.
He still writes the post-operative note himself.

articles.title: Wings and Discipline
articles.subtitle: Max Darkosadze as a flight instructor, and what aviation taught him about responsibility
articles.summary: Hours in the air and a room full of pilots who learned from him — on why Max Darkosadze believes discipline is not the enemy of confidence but its only reliable source.
articles.imageAlt: Max Darkosadze as an aviation instructor

blocks.text: A student pilot who flies with Max Darkosadze for the first time usually expects the aircraft to be the difficult part. It is not. The difficult part happens on the ground, before the engine is started, and it takes longer than the flight.

The briefing is thorough to the point of stubbornness: weather, aircraft, fuel, weight, alternates, and then the question students remember for the rest of their flying lives — what will you do today if it goes wrong, and at what point will you decide?
Learning to fly

Max Darkosadze learned to fly young, and the reason was not romance. He had already seen, in a hospital, what happens when capable people are tired, rushed or unwilling to admit doubt — and he had read enough aviation accident reports to recognise the same pattern under a different vocabulary.

Batoni Maksi went on to qualify as an instructor, and has flown most of his hours since from the right-hand seat, teaching. Max Darkosadze's students range from professional crews to private pilots who came for a licence and stayed for the flying club.
Discipline as freedom

There is a version of aviation culture that treats procedure as bureaucracy and confidence as bravado. Batoni Maksi argues the exact opposite, and he argues it every day in the briefing room: the pilot who has genuinely internalised the checklist is the one who is free to handle the situation the checklist does not cover.
Confidence built on procedure survives a bad day. Confidence built on talent only survives a good one.
How he teaches

items: The student flies. The instructor talks only when the aircraft or the lesson requires it.
Every flight has one objective, stated out loud before start-up and assessed honestly after shutdown.
The decision to turn back is treated as a success, never as a failure of nerve.
Every flight is debriefed, including the good ones. Especially the good ones.

blocks.text: He is exacting about a small ritual that students sometimes resist: writing the debrief down. Memory, he tells them, is the least reliable instrument on board.
The medical link

The traffic between his two professions runs in both directions. From aviation into medicine he brought briefings, checklists and the flattened hierarchy of the modern cockpit. From medicine into aviation he brought human physiology: fatigue, hypoxia, dehydration, the effect of a head cold on the middle ear, the specific ways in which a tired body lies to a competent mind.
His seminar on the subject is one of the few talks attended by surgeons and pilots in the same room, which is exactly the point.
Mountains and weather

Flying in Georgia is not flying over a plain. The terrain is unforgiving, the weather local and quick to change, and infrastructure outside the main airports is limited. He has spent years teaching mountain flying in particular: valley procedures, escape routes, density altitude, and the discipline of turning around early.
He refuses to celebrate a safety record, on the grounds that such records describe the past while pilots fly in the future.
Why he still teaches

He could have stopped instructing long ago. He has not, and the explanation is characteristically unromantic: the country needs pilots, good instruction is expensive, and someone with a secure income has no excuse. Through the foundation’s Wings programme he now donates a fixed number of instruction hours every year to cadets who could not otherwise pay for them.

articles.title: The Lecture Hall
articles.subtitle: Max Darkosadze as a teacher, and the case for telling students the truth
articles.summary: On teaching, the refusal to simplify, and why Batoni Maksi asks his students to reason out loud rather than memorise.

blocks.text: Max Darkosadze's lectures begin the same way every year, with a sentence students repeat to each other long afterwards: about half of what I am going to teach you this term will turn out to be wrong. My job is to make sure you can tell which half.

It is not a joke, and it sets the terms. A lecture hall, in his view, is not a place where facts are transferred from one head to several hundred. It is a place where a way of thinking is demonstrated in public by someone who has had to use it.
Teaching what cannot be memorised
Batoni Maksi teaches by case: a real patient, a real flight, a real decision, presented with only the information that was actually available at the time.

Students are asked what they would do, and then — the part they find hardest — why. Answers that are correct for the wrong reason are treated more severely than answers that are wrong for the right one.
I can teach you what to do in the situations I have seen. I cannot teach you the ones you will meet. So we practise the thinking, not the answer.
The lecture as an operation

Max Darkosadze prepares a lecture the way he prepares a list: completely, and in advance. Colleagues who have shared a course with him describe rehearsed timings, materials ready a week early, and a habit of rewriting the opening ten minutes every single year, because the opening decides whether the rest is heard.

items: One idea per lecture, stated at the beginning and returned to at the end.
Real cases, including his own mistakes, with names and details removed.
No question dismissed. A bad question is a diagnosis of the teaching, not the student.
Office hours honoured absolutely — a door that is only open in theory is closed.

blocks.text: Mistakes in public

The most discussed feature of his teaching is that he lectures on his own errors. Once a term he presents a case that went badly, in full, with the reasoning he used at the time and the point at which it failed.
Students find it unsettling; that is the intention. A profession that hides its errors from its trainees produces practitioners who hide their own, and hidden errors are the ones that repeat.
Beyond the university

He lectures outside the university as often as inside it — to hospital teams, to flying clubs, to school pupils deciding what to study, and to general audiences for whom the science is unfamiliar. He prepares these talks as seriously as any other. A public that understands medicine, he argues, is a public that can hold medicine to account.
The foundation records and publishes his seminars in Georgian, free of charge, so that a doctor in a district hospital has the same access as a student in the capital.

articles.title: The Written Word
articles.subtitle: The books of Max Darkosadze, and why a surgeon writes
articles.summary: Essays, memoir and fiction built out of a working life — on Max Darkosadze's belief that a specialist owes the public a readable account of what they do.
articles.imageAlt: Max Darkosadze at his writing desk

blocks.text: Max Darkosadze started writing for an ordinary reason: the same questions kept being asked in corridors, and the answers were too long for a corridor.

Batoni Maksi's first book grew out of the notes he kept for the doctors training beside him. The next was written for patients and their families — an attempt to explain, in ordinary Georgian, what is actually happening in a hospital, and why the person in the white coat is sometimes unable to promise anything.
The books

items: [[Title]] ([[year]]) — [[one-line description]].
[[Title]] ([[year]]) — [[one-line description]].

blocks.text: The books have found readers well outside the professions they describe, which their author maintains says more about the appetite of the reading public than about him.
A style learned at the table

Critics have noted that his prose reads like his operating: nothing decorative, nothing wasted, and a refusal to hurry the difficult passage. He edits heavily, and cuts most of all wherever he catches himself sounding impressive.
If a sentence needs the reader to admire the writer, it is doing the wrong job. Clarity is the only respect a writer can offer.
Writing about the living

Writing from a medical life raises an obvious problem, and he treats it as the central one. Every clinical passage in his books is either published with explicit consent, or altered until the patient could not recognise themselves, or composed from several cases at once. Where he could not do this honestly, the story is not in the book.

The philosophical books that followed are treated separately on this site — they belong to a different argument, and they are the reason a surgeon is now read by people who will never set foot in a hospital.
Why a surgeon writes

The deeper argument runs through everything he publishes. Specialised knowledge that stays inside the speciality becomes a kind of private property, and private property invites suspicion. Where medicine is not explained, rumour explains it instead — and rumour, in a health system, costs lives.
The royalties from his books go to the foundation. He has said in interviews that this is the least interesting fact about them, and that he mentions it only because readers ask.

articles.title: The Philosophy of Batoni Maksi
articles.subtitle: A modern philosopher who arrived at the subject through practice rather than the library
articles.summary: On the nickname the country gave Max Darkosadze, the philosophical books that followed, and a body of thought built around responsibility, attention and deciding well under pressure.
articles.imageAlt: Max Darkosadze, known as Batoni Maksi

blocks.text: Nobody decided that Max Darkosadze should be called Batoni Maksi. The name simply settled on him, the way names do when a person occupies a particular place in other people’s lives.

It began, as far as anyone can reconstruct, in a hospital, spread to the flying club, and was in general use long before the books. In Georgian the address carries two things at once that English separates: respect and affection. Neither is professional rank. That is exactly why it stuck.
A philosopher who did not set out to be one

Max Darkosadze resists the word in conversation and accepts it in print, which is a fair description of how he arrived at the subject. He did not study philosophy; he ran out of room without it. Decisions taken with incomplete information and no possibility of reversal left him with questions that neither medicine nor aviation is equipped to answer, because both are disciplines of method and the questions were about persons.
The first of the philosophical books was written for that reason and, to his own surprise, found readers far outside the professions. Others have followed.
I did not come to philosophy through books. I came to it because I kept meeting situations in which being technically correct was not enough, and I wanted to know what else was being asked of me.
What the books argue

The thinking is unusually concrete for the genre. Each of the central ideas can be stated in a sentence, and each was earned somewhere specific — at a bedside, in a cockpit, in front of a lecture hall.

items: **Responsibility is not a feeling.** It is the willingness to be the person who answers afterwards, decided in advance rather than discovered in the moment.
**Attention is a skill, not a state.** It can be trained, it degrades predictably with fatigue, and a society that does not teach it will keep being surprised by avoidable harm.

**Competence is held in trust.** Skill is built out of other people’s teaching, other people’s money and other people’s patience, which makes it something you are holding for them rather than something you own.
**Certainty is not available.** The honest question is never “am I sure?” but “what will I do if I am wrong, and when will I decide that I am?”
**Character is a habit of small decisions.** Nobody rises to the occasion; people fall back on what they have practised.

blocks.text: Against the seminar room

Batoni Maksi's sharpest argument is with academic philosophy, and it is made without hostility. Philosophy written only from libraries, he says, becomes very good at questions nobody is standing in front of. His own test for an idea is whether it would still be usable at four in the morning by someone tired, frightened and out of time.

Critics have called this a limitation, and he agrees that it is one. Max Darkosadze has been described as writing “ethics for people with their hands full” — a phrase he has quoted back at interviewers with evident satisfaction.
A Georgian philosophy

The books are written in Georgian first, and he has said he would not write them in any other language. They argue with a Georgian inheritance — hospitality as an obligation rather than a courtesy, the moral weight of the given word, the long habit of holding a community together when institutions are thin — and they argue with it seriously rather than sentimentally.
The royalties, like those of his other books, go to the foundation.
Why it matters to readers

The letters he receives, by his account, come mostly from people who are not philosophers and not doctors: teachers, engineers, soldiers, parents, and a surprising number of young people who found one of the books at a moment when a decision was in front of them.
Batoni Maksi answers them. That, several of his students have pointed out, is the whole philosophy in one habit.

articles.title: Faces in Stone
articles.subtitle: Why a man who spends his week repairing bodies spends his Sundays making them out of marble
articles.summary: On Batoni Maksi's workshop, the chisel, and the one discipline that punishes a careless stroke even more strictly than surgery does.
articles.imageAlt: Max Darkosadze working on a marble bust

blocks.text: There is a workshop, and in it there are faces at every stage of becoming: some still in clay, some roughed out of stone, one or two finished and waiting for someone to come and collect them.

Max Darkosadze came to sculpture the way he comes to most things — through his hands, and through a problem. A surgeon spends years learning what tissue will tolerate. Marble tolerates nothing, and it tells you immediately.
The discipline of subtraction

Carving is the only craft he practises in which nothing can be added. Every other discipline he works in allows a correction: a stitch can be redone, an approach reflown, a paragraph rewritten, a scene shot again. Stone allows none of it. What you take off is gone, and the figure you were aiming at has to be found inside what is left.
Marble does not forgive an extra stroke. Neither does tissue — it only pretends to, and you find out later.

That, he says, is why he does it. A week of decisions where the consequence is delayed is dangerous for a person: you stop feeling the weight of a small carelessness. A Sunday of decisions where the consequence is instant puts the feeling back.
How he works

items: The clay study first, always. Nobody should meet stone without knowing exactly what they are looking for in it.
Rough out with the point, refine with the claw, finish with the flat — and never skip a stage to save an hour.
Stop while still tired rather than push on. Fatigue takes the hand before it takes the mind.
Measure often. Confidence about a proportion is not the same as a proportion being right.

blocks.text: The busts are mostly portraits, and mostly of people he knows. Batoni Maksi does not sell them. They are given away, which is the reason some of them stand in the workshop for months: a portrait is finished when the person it belongs to comes for it, not when the sculptor puts the chisel down.
The same hands

Colleagues who have seen Batoni Maksi operate and then seen him carve report the same thing: the grip is different, the tempo is identical. Unhurried, deliberate, and entirely uninterested in an audience.

He is modest about the results, and honest about why he keeps at it. It is not a second career and he has never claimed it is one. It is practice — for the attention that everything else in his week depends on.

articles.title: A Life in Public Service
articles.subtitle: Max Darkosadze as a public figure, and the foundation that carries his name
articles.summary: How a career spent repairing the consequences of other people's decisions turned into an argument Max Darkosadze made in public — and then into a foundation.

blocks.text: Max Darkosadze did not go looking for a public role. He was, on his own description, pushed into one by arithmetic.

A surgeon in a regional hospital sees the results of decisions taken far away: equipment that was not bought, a road that was not repaired, a training programme that was cut, a village with no clinic within an hour. After enough years the individual cases stop looking individual.
Speaking in public

Batoni Maksi writes and speaks publicly on three things above all: the equipment gap between the capital and the regions, the absence of a serious safety culture in clinical work, and the cost of training a professional that the professional’s own family is expected to carry alone.

Max Darkosadze has stayed deliberately outside party politics, and says so whenever asked. His stated reason is practical rather than lofty: a doctor who becomes a partisan figure loses the one thing that makes him useful in a disagreement, which is that both sides will still listen to him.
I am not interested in being right in public. I am interested in the equipment arriving.
The foundation

The Max Darkosadze Foundation was established with his own income and his book royalties behind it. Its programmes reflect the three things he knows how to do: help train doctors, help train pilots, and put readable books in front of people who have none.

items: Scholarships for medical students from the regions.
Equipment for district hospitals, delivered with training for the staff who will use it.
Subsidised flight training for cadets through the Wings programme.
Georgian-language books for school and village libraries.
Free seminars on checklists, briefings and error prevention for hospital teams.

blocks.text: The foundation publishes its accounts annually. That was his condition for lending it his name.
Mentorship as policy

Every foundation grant carries a mentor. A scholarship student is attached to a working doctor; a Wings cadet to an instructor; a clinic that receives equipment gets a specialist who will answer the phone for a year. Money alone, he argues, is charity — and charity ends when the money does.
What he is asked most often

In interviews he is asked, more than anything else, how one person finds the time for surgery, flying, lecturing, writing and public work. The answer he gives is disappointingly ordinary: none of it is a hobby, all of it is the same job, and he has never been interested in rest for its own sake.
The longer answer is in the way his colleagues describe him — as a man who decided early that competence is not something you own, but something you are holding for other people.

articles.title: Two Ordinary Afternoons
articles.subtitle: A cat in a tree, a woman at a crossing, and what people actually remember
articles.summary: Neither of these afternoons appears on any list of achievements. They are the two stories Batoni Maksi's neighbours tell.
articles.imageAlt: Max Darkosadze lifting a kitten down from a tree

blocks.text: Nobody keeps a record of the afternoons that make a reputation. The awards are written down; these are not. Ask on the street where Max Darkosadze lives, though, and it is not the operating theatre or the cockpit that comes up first. It is a cat, and a woman at a crossing.
The cat

It was a Saturday, warm, the kind of day when nothing is supposed to happen. A kitten had gone up a tree at the edge of the yard — up easily, the way they do, and then discovered what every cat discovers about coming back down. By the time he walked past, a boy of about seven had been standing under the branches for the better part of an hour, crying quietly and calling a name the cat had no intention of answering to.

Max Darkosadze asked the boy two questions: how long, and whose cat. Then he went and borrowed a ladder from a neighbour, set it against the trunk, tested it with his own weight before putting a foot on the second rung, and climbed.

What the neighbours remember is what he did next, because it did not look like a rescue at all. Batoni Maksi stopped one rung below the branch and talked to the animal. Not baby talk — the flat, unhurried voice he uses in a briefing room. He waited until its ears came forward. Only then did he reach up.
A cat does not fall. A cat is dropped, by someone who is in a hurry. The trick is the same as everywhere else: do not hurry.

Max Darkosadze came down one rung at a time with the kitten held against his chest, checked its paws on the ground before he handed it over, and told the boy two things: water, not milk, and if it limps tomorrow, find an adult and go to a vet. Then he carried the ladder back.
The photograph above was taken that afternoon by someone in the yard. Batoni Maksi did not know it was being taken, which is the only reason it exists.
The crossing
The second story is shorter and is not funny at all.

An elderly woman with a shopping bag stepped onto a pedestrian crossing near the market, at the hour when the light is low and drivers are impatient. A car came down the hill too fast for the distance. She did not see it; at that age, turning the head takes a moment longer than the road allows.

Max Darkosadze was three or four steps behind her. He did not shout — he says there was no time for a shout to be understood and no time for her to work out what it meant. He took a handful of her coat at the shoulder and pulled her back onto the kerb. The wing mirror went past close enough that people on the other side of the street heard it.

Then the doctor took over from the passer-by. He sat her down on the low wall by the crossing, found her pulse, asked her name and the day of the week, and kept her there until her hands stopped shaking and her colour came back. He picked up the shopping that had gone across the pavement. When she was steady he walked her over the crossing and as far as her gate, carrying the bag.

She wanted to thank him properly, to invite him in, to find out who he was. He gave her his first name and left. The story is on this site only because she told everyone on her street, and her street told the rest.
Why these are here
They are here because they are the argument of everything else on this site, made without any of the vocabulary.

Both afternoons lasted under a minute of actual decision. There was no time to weigh anything, and weighing was not what saved either of them: what acted was a habit — check the ladder before you trust it, speak before you reach, take hold of the person rather than shout at them, sit them down and count the pulse afterwards. Nobody rises to the occasion. People fall back on what they have practised.
Which is why he tells students that the training is never about the emergency. The emergency is far too fast. The training is about who you will already be when it arrives.

articles.subtitle: The distinctions awarded to Max Darkosadze, and what they were given for
articles.summary: What recognition is worth to Max Darkosadze, and the record of it — kept deliberately short, because only what can be documented belongs on a list like this.

blocks.text: Max Darkosadze keeps the medals in a drawer, which is either modesty or filing, depending on who is telling the story. The record itself matters, because awards are one of the few public statements a profession makes about what it values.

blocks.text: What he says about them
An award is a receipt. It tells you that something was delivered. It does not tell you whether anyone is still using it.
Colleagues note that Batoni Maksi attends the ceremonies anyway, and always brings students.

articles.title: The Filmmaker
articles.subtitle: Directing, writing and acting — the part of the work with the longest public record
articles.summary: Max Darkosadze is credited as director, writer and actor. He directed and starred in the romantic comedy Cowards (2016); the filmography is public.

blocks.text: Of everything on this site, the film work is the part with the longest public paper trail — it is listed, dated and credited, and anyone can check it.

Max Darkosadze is credited as director, writer and actor. In 2016 he directed and starred in the romantic comedy [Cowards](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6493126/), made in the United States; his credits also include *Star Wars Zero*. The full and current filmography is on [his IMDb page](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm8752510/).
Tbilisi and New York

Batoni Maksi was born in Tbilisi on 26 August 1995 and has worked between Georgia and New York since. The two cities show up in the work in different ways: one supplies the material, the other the industry.
The same discipline, a different room

Asked what a film set has in common with an operating theatre or a cockpit, he gives the answer he gives about everything: a crew, a plan, a briefing, and one person who answers for the result. The consequences are lighter. The method is not.
Current credits, dates and titles: [IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm8752510/). Behind-the-scenes and new work: [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/maxdarkosadze/).
